newsitem.title: USA: Health industry gears up for Medicare budget battle.
newsitem.headline: Health industry gears up for Medicare budget battle.

text.p: Doctors, hospitals, managed care plans and other health providers are preparing to duke it out as Congress writes legislation to fill in the details of a five-year balanced budget deal making major cuts in Medicare.

The long-sought agreement worked out between the White House and congressional Republicans last week calls for $115 billion in Medicare reductions to help balance the budget and ensure the 10-year solvency of the popular insurance programme.

About $100 billion of overall Medicare savings will come from cutting federal payments to the health care industry. But negotiators only agreed on outlines, leaving it to lawmakers to fill in the blanks -- and leaving it to interest groups to lobby Congress.
"Everything is more or less on the table," Richard Pollack, executive vice president of the American Hospitial Association said.

Decisions made in coming weeks will have a major impact on the industry's bottom line. They will also affect the quality and availability of health care to the 38 million senior citizens across the nation who rely on Medicare.

After the pitched battles of the recent years, there is consensus between Republicans and Democrats on Medicare reforms such as payment controls on the fast-growing home health industry, a cut or freeze in payments to hospitals, anti-fraud measures and reductions in managed care payments.
The challenge for industry groups is to minimise the pain.

Managed care plans warn they may have to raise premiums or trim services to seniors if payments are cut too sharply. Hospitals seek power to band with doctors to offer a new type of health plan, with exemptions from state regulation.

Republicans want to expand the range of health plans available to Medicare recipients. They will push for malpractice reform and may try to add tax-free medical savings accounts as an option under Medicare.

"Based on what I've seen so far, I believe (Medicare) has been strengthened" in the budget deal, Gail Shearer of the Consumers Union said. "We will be very active if necessary in fighting any proposals for medical savings accounts."

The reason providers are taking such a big hit is simple politics. Fearing the wrath of seniors who rely on Medicare, Clinton and the Republicans did everything they could to avoid big increases in monthly premiums or out-of-pocket costs.

The budget will freeze the Part B premium for doctors' care, now $43.80 per month, at 25 percent of programme costs rather than letting it fall as planned. Premiums will also rise slightly to cover the costs of home health services.
The deal adds new preventive benefits like mammograms and diabetes screening. A plan to provide respite care for families of Alzheimer's patients was dropped.

Republicans and Democrats disagreed publicly Wednesday about whether the budget deal includes a provision giving low-income Medicare beneficiaries more protection from paying higher premiums. The White House insisted it did, while Republicans said it was a detail to be worked out by Congress.
"We have to be cautious because so much of the important stuff is still to be decided," said John Rother of the American Association of Retired Persons.

Clinton's original budget called for major cuts to managed care plans, which the White House argues are overpaid. Industry officials say if Congress does not reduce the hit, they will have to cut services to Medicare patients.
"Everybody is ready to get down and roll up their sleeves and work on a policy that's more equitable," Kristin Bass of the American Association of Health Plans said.
Hospitals are fighting a freeze or cut in annual Medicare payments and fret about changes in financing for graduate medical education.

But the American Hospital Association also hopes Congress will give hospitals the power to band with doctors to set up provider-sponsored organisations to compete with managed care. Lawmakers and the White House both support the change, a key question is whether states will regulate the new plans.
"We think it's a very high priority to have PSOs provided in this and we think we've got an agreement to do just that," a White House official said.

Another industry effected by the budget is home health -- one of the fastest growing parts of Medicare. Both Congress and the White House want tighter payment controls to hold down the cost of home health services. To help keep Medicare solvent, the budget shifts $86 billion in home health services out of the troubled hospital trust fund and into the doctors programme.
